summary: This document is an implementation report for the RPKI Router protocol defined in RFC 6810. The authors did not verify the respondents' answers, but the respondents are experts on the implementations they described.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a survey asking different makers whether their products really follow a rulebook. The answers were collected and listed, but not double-checked.

subtitle: A survey of how different vendors implement the RPKI Router protocol.

tldr.problem: The RPKI Router protocol lets routers fetch validated prefix origin data, but there was no clarity on how well different vendors had implemented it.
tldr.mechanism: This report collects implementation details from vendors who built RPKI Router clients and servers, including which features they support, how they handle errors, and how they interoperate.
tldr.outcome: The report documents that major vendors like Cisco, Juniper, and others have working implementations that can interoperate with different cache servers.

today: RFC 7128 is an Informational document that documents the state of RPKI Router implementations as of early 2014. The protocol itself is now defined in RFC 6810. The interoperability findings remain relevant as these core implementations continue to be deployed.

sections.title: Why This Report Matters
sections.content:
The RPKI Router protocol (defined in RFC 6810) is how routers get trusted information about which Autonomous Systems (ASes) are allowed to announce which IP prefixes. Before this report, vendors had built implementations, but there was no public documentation of how complete or compatible they were.

This report is an implementation survey: the authors asked representatives from six major vendors and projects (Cisco IOS, Cisco IOS-XR, Juniper JUNOS, rpki.net, RIPE NCC, and RTRlib) to fill out a form describing what parts of the protocol they had built. The authors did not independently verify the answers, but the respondents are experts in their own implementations and their responses are authoritative for those products.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors asked six companies: do you have the RPKI Router feature? How much of it? Can you talk to other vendors' systems? They trusted the experts at those companies to answer honestly.

sections.title: Implementation Forms
sections.content:
RPKI Router implementations come in two flavors: client (a router that fetches prefix origin data) and server (a cache that stores and serves that data). Cisco's IOS and IOS-XR are routers, so they are clients. The RIPE NCC validator and BBN RPSTIR are servers that provide data to clients. Some projects like rpki.net built both: a client library and a server.

The respondents are experts on routers and cache software from the time the survey was conducted (early 2014). Their implementations had been tested in the lab by their authors before being reported as working, so 'YES' means at least lab-tested, not necessarily production-deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems are routers (they ask for the data) and some are caches (they give the data). This report lists which ones were ready for testing at the time.

sections.title: Protocol Messages and Data Units
sections.content:
The RPKI Router protocol uses 11 types of message, called Protocol Data Units (PDUs). The main ones are Serial Notify (to say 'data changed'), Serial Query (to ask for changes), Reset Query (to ask for a full reload), and the answer messages: Cache Response (here is the zone serial), IPv4 and IPv6 Prefix (a prefix origin rule), and End of Data (that is all). An Error Report PDU lets either side report a problem.

The table shows that all major implementations support the most important ones: clients can receive IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, serial notify and end of data. All client implementations support Serial Query and Reset Query. Only rpki.net and RIPE NCC as servers can originate (send) Serial Notify. The one anomaly is JUNOS, which does not receive or send the Error PDU; when it encounters an error it just disconnects.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has eleven message types. The table shows whether each router and cache can send and receive each type. Most vendors support most messages, with a few exceptions for error handling.

sections.title: How Implementations Handle Key Features
sections.content:
The protocol defines four typical message sequences: Start or Restart, Typical Exchange (incremental updates), No Incremental Update Available, and Cache Has No Data. All implementations handle all four sequences correctly, with one exception: the RIPE NCC validator does not implement the Serial Query request, so it always responds by resetting (sending all data again) when asked for incremental updates.

A critical feature is support for incremental updates. When the cache's data changes, a client can ask only for what changed rather than reloading everything. Clients from Cisco do not support this; Juniper and rpki.net do. On the transport side, TCP is universal, but SSH is only in rpki.net, some Cisco IOS-XR deployments, RTRlib, and BBN RPSTIR. No implementation supports TLS, TCP-MD5, TCP-AO, or IPsec for the router-to-cache connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The different implementations handle updates in different ways. Most let routers ask for just what changed, but Cisco does not. All use plain TCP, and only a few support SSH encryption.

sections.title: Interoperability
sections.content:
The report documents interoperability testing that vendors carried out. Cisco IOS and IOS-XR have been tested with rpki.net. Juniper JUNOS has been tested with both rpki.net and RIPE NCC cache servers. The rpki.net implementation has been tested with Cisco clients from both vendors. RIPE NCC tested with RTRlib and Cisco IOS; they also received positive feedback from contacts who tested with JUNOS and Quagga. RTRlib (from Hamburg University) tested with rpki.net and RIPE NCC.

One implementation, BBN RPSTIR, had not been tested with other vendors' products at the time of the report. The overall picture shows that the major vendor implementations can interoperate, giving operators confidence that they can mix and match cache software with router products from different vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: The vendors tested their routers with different caches to make sure they work together. Most combinations worked. This means network operators can choose any router and any cache and they should work.

references.text: Bush, R. and R. Austein, "The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) to Router Protocol", RFC 6810, January 2013.
